reasoning.Student A:
I assume the standard student-proposing deferred acceptance mechanism (where truthful ranking is a dominant strategy). Given that, I should report my true preferences.

Key points:
- My true preference order is y > x > w > z, so I rank schools in that order.
- I have top priority (rank 1) at y (and also at w). That makes it very likely I will obtain y if I list it first — so there is no advantage to misreporting.
- Although w also gives me top priority, I prefer x over w; under DA, putting x ahead of w does not harm my prospects at y (my top choice) and is the truthful strategy to try for x before settling for w.
- Most applicants also favor y > x > w > z, but because I have priority 1 at y, competition from others does not change that truthful ranking is best.

Therefore I will submit my true ranking: y > x > w > z.

I prefer z > y > x > w. Key strategic facts:
- I have top priority (1) at x and z, lower priority (2) at y and w.
- Most other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so y is highly contested and z is relatively uncontested.
If the matching uses the standard student-proposing deferred-acceptance mechanism (strategy-proof for students), it is optimal to report my true preferences. Given my high priority at z and the low popularity of z among others, listing z first is both truthful and safe. y is my second choice but more competitive (and I have lower priority there), so it should be listed after z. x is a decent backup because I also have priority 1 there, and w last.
(If the mechanism were not strategy-proof—for example, the Boston mechanism—one might consider ranking a “safe” school like x first to avoid early-round rejection at a popular reach like y; but absent that, truth-telling is the best strategy.)
